whisper.text:
The very first recording of an off-axis hologram was made in March 1961 and at that time we didn't have a laser, so we used mercury arc lamps and semi-coherent light sources. And Emmet was writing his paper, Communication Theory and Optics, and making some photographic illustrations. And the one we couldn't do was to demonstrate the off-axis hologram. But then I was in the laboratory. There was a paper that described how a Runcke-Ruhlin, when it imaged and when you block some of the diffracted lines in the transform plane, that it changed the sharpness and how the image changed. So while looking at that I thought, well what happens if I select only two points from those and over ten diffracted spots? And of course there was light. And I was in the laboratory. And I was in the laboratory. And I was in the laboratory. And I was in the laboratory. It looked like interference lines. And it was very contrasty all across the field. So then I selected these two points and placed a very fine copper wire near the focus point just where before the two beams overlapped. And then made a recording in the image plane. So that was the first off-axis hologram. Then in 1962 we tried to make some more holograms and then the first laser came around and we had my colleague, Bud Vanderloot, had managed to buy one of the first lasers which was really expensive, something like $10,000 and he was in the adjoining room so we put in a mirror and borrowed the beam to our optical bench in the adjoining room and then with that we could make the first holograms of transparencies, of continuous tone transparencies and those were published in the second paper. When this paper appeared in December 1963, the Physical Society of America released a press release about the holograms and Emmett received many telephone calls inquiring about it. It was kind of… Headline was… Lensless photography, something like that and when he answered the interviews he added, by the way, that we could also record three-dimensional object, two images and the reporters certainly didn't believe it that if he had done it and he hadn't but he kind of said, well, it was obvious that you could do that. But they certainly doubted that. So in their reports they never mentioned that holograms were three-dimensional, could record three-dimensional images. Right after that we immediately went to the lab and started to set up to record a reflective hologram of this little train that we borrowed from one of our technicians in the laboratory and at first we didn't get any results. There were stability problems and… I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. The beams were not equalized, reference and object beams were not equalized. So at first we just got blank films but then in the last week of December 1963 we finally succeeded in making one good hologram, four by five inch hologram of this little train and we were really excited to see that because it was so realistic. It was… Even though we knew it should be realistic but it was something else to see it. And then once we saw it we also started showing other colleagues in the laboratory and then the management. So we had a continuous stream of people coming and looking.

This is what we used to do on a table that was like 4 feet by 8 feet or 5 by 10. I don't know what it was, but it was a huge sandbox. And... The sandbox was a huge sandbox. It was a huge sandbox. The sandbox then allowed us to sink things in and lock them down. But the problem with the sandbox is sand. And it's dirty and it affects the optics, right? And you can see that the laser is a glowing tube. And it's a tube that is really composed of neon. Neon gas with a dose of helium. That's why it's called a helium neon laser. There we go. But shortly, a couple of years after, with this continuous wave laser, you were able to make holograms, transmission holograms, like Leithen and Patnicks did, using a borrowed beam of a continuous wave laser. So I used this beam splitter, essentially, to split the beam in half. Part of it is here. There, yeah. See? Yep. The beam comes through. And part of it is reflected here. Can you get that in a picture? Yep. And this laser is essentially a spectrophysics model. And its output is rated about 15 milliwatts. And you can run it hot like we did. 20 milliwatts. And, you know, what I found really cool is that when this sucker fired up, it was just like the same laser we used at Visual Alchemy in the 1970s. 47 years ago. So if it was 1974 and you saw what some of the sandbox optics were, 1974. Yeah. So if it was 1974 and you saw what some of the sandbox optics were, 1974. 1974 we had a big sandbox, 8 feet by 4 feet at Visual Alchemy. And we had this laser tube. And that was a tough way to make holography and then put it on display, which meant that we had to have little lasers for illuminating the transmission holograms for display. And you could only afford so many of them. So from transmission holograms, which are my favorite, we went to reflection holograms, which were the Denisov method, the Russian method developed. And then we used theater lights, spotlights. Big kick-ass spotlights. So this beautiful little helium neon laser, now it's without its cover so we can see the tube, is going to be sold, as an antique. But fuck, it's like the kind of antique that Michelangelo might have used to chisel his, you know, David, right? Yeah. Here's the hammer that Michelangelo used. Here's the laser that Sharon McCormick used in her lab. And presumably Lloyd Cross used. It's almost exactly the same as the one that Al Rizutis used in Visual Alchemy, in the same 70s. Very cool. Very cool, yeah. And it's a wonderful invention. And now, you know, lasers are used everywhere. When you scan a barcode, you've got a laser.
